title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 6: Does the MNLF Have International Legal Personality?
keywords: Does the MNLF Have International Legal Personality?
Reparations for Injuries Suffered in the Service of the United States
Mindanao, Sulu, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi and Palawan
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- the legal opinion Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban rendered at the request of former Ambassador Melchor P. Aquino on the international-law effects of the Philippine government's agreeing to meet the MNLF in a third country under the auspices of the Organization of the Islamic Conference.

His core answer: the Jeddah meeting and accord did not substantially alter his earlier opinion that, under traditional international law, the MNLF (and the NDF) has not been accorded a status of belligerency.

His warning nonetheless: because international law is fast evolving and recognition is a political act beyond judicial review, acquiescing to meet outside Philippine territory under OIC auspices could supply excuses for vesting 'quasi' international personality in the MNLF and warranting intervention in what would otherwise be a domestic affair.

The closing concession that peace is worth the risk -- he does not blame the government for its quest, since success would justify the brinkmanship and failure would at least leave the satisfaction of having exhausted all avenues.
sub_topics: The factual background: Minister Aquilino Pimentel, having announced that the government preferred all talks be held in the Philippines, left unceremoniously for Jeddah on December 30, 1986 with panel members Agapito 'Butz' Aquino and Norberto Gonzales and Deputy Minister Saidamen Pangarungan, pursuant to a ceasefire signed in a Jolo convent.

The January 3, 1987 Jeddah agreement under the auspices of the 46-member Organization of the Islamic Conference, in which the MNLF dropped its demand for full independence and agreed to negotiate autonomy -- which chairman Nur Misuari said would mean a 'state within a state' -- for Mindanao, Sulu, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi and Palawan.

The query put by Ambassador Aquino: what are the effects in international law of meeting MNLF representatives in a third country under the auspices of an association of 46 states to which the Philippines does not belong?

His earlier opinion restated -- that neither the MNLF nor the NDF had a status of belligerency -- with the caveat that there is no purely legal right to be recognized, so that recognition is discretionary, political in character, and can hardly be questioned in an international legal tribunal.

The estoppel point: this was not the first such meeting, since the Tripoli Agreement of 1977 was concluded in Libya by the Marcos government in like circumstances, so refusal now would not have prevented third states from finding political justifications, and the present government is estopped from denouncing the previous regime's acts.

The comparative illustrations: it is difficult to imagine Great Britain negotiating with the Irish Republican Army in Italy or Spain under the auspices of an association of Catholic states, or India meeting Sikh separatists in a third state sponsored by a body it does not belong to -- though Philippine practice has made the thought academic.

The doctrinal history: traditionally only sovereign states were subjects of international law, and in the days of Grotius only states had international personality; the concept has since changed so that other entities possess personality even if incomplete, imperfect, qualified or quasi, as the International Court of Justice recognized in its Reparations advisory opinion.

The evolutionary argument: international law is not imposed by a political superior but derives from the collective acts or agreements of states, and in fifty years more than 100 new states have emerged and challenged traditional doctrines -- so that absolute illegality of intervention in domestic affairs has yielded exceptions, as when India used large-scale military force in Pakistan in 1971 over East Bengal.

The summary holding and the reservation: belligerency has not been accorded to the Muslim insurgents, but the acts of acquiescence are frowned upon because 46 states could by agreement spawn new principles justifying recognition and eventual direct intervention.

The concluding qualification: he is not privy to the government's reasons, the MNLF's dropping of independence does not minimize the role of Saudi Arabia and the OIC but gives them a more permanent role, yet peace must be pursued regardless of legal and political niceties.

stances.claim: He does not blame the government for its quest for peace: if the attempt succeeds the brinkmanship will have been worth it, and if it fails the government will at least have exhausted all avenues, because peace must be pursued regardless of legal and political niceties.

notable_anecdotes: The unceremonious departure: he sets the scene with Pimentel announcing that the government prefers all talks be held in the Philippines and not the Middle East, then leaving for Jeddah days later on December 30, 1986.
The Jolo convent: the Jeddah meeting is traced to a ceasefire agreement signed a few months earlier in a convent in Jolo, Sulu.

The IRA and Sikh hypotheticals: he tests the propriety of the venue by imagining Great Britain negotiating with the Irish Republican Army in Italy or Spain under an association of Catholic states, and India meeting Sikh separatists in Nepal under a body it does not belong to.

The East Bengal precedent: he cites India's 1971 use of large-scale military force in Pakistan, justified by allegations of killings, imprisonment and mass refugee flights, as proof that the absolute bar on intervention in domestic affairs has given way.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reproduces the legal opinion Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban rendered at the request of former Ambassador to Germany and Manila Bulletin columnist Melchor P. Aquino, printed in full in the Bulletin on January 14, 1987. The facts he sets out are that Minister Aquilino Pimentel, head of the Philippine panel negotiating with the MNLF, had announced that the government preferred all talks to be held in the Philippines and not the Middle East, yet left unceremoniously for Jeddah on December 30, 1986 with panel members Agapito 'Butz' Aquino and Norberto Gonzales and Deputy Minister Saidamen Pangarungan, pursuant to a ceasefire signed in a Jolo convent; on January 3, 1987 an agreement was signed under the auspices of the 46-member Organization of the Islamic Conference, the MNLF dropping its demand for full independence and agreeing to negotiate autonomy that chairman Nur Misuari said would mean a 'state within a state' for Mindanao, Sulu, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi and Palawan. Asked what the international-law effects of meeting in a third country under such auspices were, Panganiban restated his earlier opinion that neither the MNLF nor the NDF had a status of belligerency, subject to the caveat that there is no purely legal right to be recognized, so recognition is discretionary, political, and hardly reviewable in an international tribunal. He observed that the practice was not new -- the Tripoli Agreement of 1977 was concluded in Libya by the Marcos government -- so that refusal would have prevented nothing and the present government is estopped from denouncing the prior regime, though he doubted Britain would meet the IRA, or India Sikh separatists, on comparable terms. Tracing the doctrine from Grotius, when only states had international personality, through the ICJ's Reparations advisory opinion recognizing action by entities that are not states, he stressed that international law derives from the collective acts of states and has evolved -- more than 100 new states in fifty years, and exceptions now allowing humanitarian intervention, as with India in East Bengal in 1971. He concluded that belligerency had not been accorded, but frowned upon acquiescing to meet outside Philippine territory under OIC auspices, warning that 46 states could by agreement spawn new principles vesting 'quasi' personality in the MNLF and warranting intervention in a domestic affair. Still, he refused to blame the government, holding that peace must be pursued regardless of legal and political niceties.
